title: The hazelnut
hook: Julian of Norwich sees all that is made as small as a hazelnut in her palm, lasting because it is loved (Revelations of Divine Love 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brother Lawrence in the kitchen, turning the omelette for love. Your line was the kitchen is enough. Which chore did you do slowly? Day eighty-eight.

You've probably seen the famous photo of Earth taken from far out in space: a tiny pale dot, almost lost in a beam of light. People who see it often say the same thing. Everything is on there. Everyone who ever lived. Every war, every wedding, every lunch. And it's so small. Six centuries before any camera left the planet, a woman in England, very sick and close to death, saw something like that, except it was sitting in the palm of her hand. Today's story is the hazelnut.
screen: `A PALE DOT IN SPACE.` → `EVERYTHING, AND SO SMALL.` → `SOMETHING IN HER PALM.`

segments.voice: In May of 1373, a woman in Norwich, in England, was thirty and a half years old and so ill that everyone expected her to die. A priest held a crucifix in front of her eyes. And over the next hours she received what she called sixteen showings, visions about the love of God. She recovered. She wrote them down, and then spent some twenty years thinking about them and wrote them again, longer. That book, Revelations of Divine Love, is often called the first book in English known to be written by a woman. We don't know her real name. She lived as an anchoress, in a small room attached to the church of Saint Julian in Norwich, and people called her Julian after the church. Early in the book, she says she was shown a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, lying in the palm of her hand, round as a ball. She looked at it and wondered what it could be. And the answer came, in Grace Warrack's old translation: "It is all that is made." Everything. The whole created world, in one palm. And she marveled how it could last, because it seemed so small it might just fall into nothing. And she understood: it lasts, and always will, because God loves it. She saw three things in that little ball: God made it, God loves it, God keeps it. Many Christians treasure this as one of the tenderest pictures of creation they know. For anyone, it's a way of looking at small things. A stone, a cup, a hand. Small enough to fall into nothing. Still here.
screen: `NORWICH, MAY 1373.` · `SIXTEEN SHOWINGS.` · `A HAZELNUT IN HER PALM.` · `MADE, LOVED, KEPT.` · then, large: `ALL THAT IS MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something small and look. Pick up something small that's near you: a coin, a button, a pebble, a nut, a ring. If there's nothing, look at your own open palm. Settle, and breathe. Let it rest in your hand. Look at it for longer than feels normal. Notice its color, its edges, its weight. Notice how easily it could be lost. And notice that it's here anyway. If you pray, you can hold Julian's three words: made, loved, kept. The bell holds the time.
The hazelnut. Julian's vision of everything that is made, small enough to sit in her palm, lasting because it is loved. Today's word.
Your line: all that is made. Today, pick up one small thing, a leaf, a cup, a stone, and look at it as if the whole world were in your hand. Day eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians of many churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love as a classic of prayer, and the Anglican, Lutheran and Episcopal calendars remember her each May.
